video_title: The AI Crash Is Over. Here's What Comes Next
gist: Jordi Visser calls the AI factor 'speed crash' over — the bottom is in — citing a ~10% four-day Nasdaq rally, collapsing factor volatility, new all-time highs in IWM/NYSE Composite/equal-weight S&P, and ~50% earnings growth, and argues index puts no longer hedge an AI book because factor vol has structurally decoupled from index vol. He pairs that with a debasement thesis: the first coordinated US-Japan yen intervention since 1998, Bessent leaning on the Fed, and a weak-but-unrecognized US labor market make gold, silver, platinum and Bitcoin the trades, while AI-native one-person companies erode Fortune 500 profits by 2030.

insights.claim: Jordi Visser declares the AI-factor 'speed crash' finished and the bottom in on a probability basis, saying he would be surprised if the lows are taken out because investors are far too bearish relative to incoming earnings growth.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Frames the recent AI-factor washout as a buyable cleansing event rather than the start of a bear market; the prior lows become the risk-management line.
insights.quote: The speed crash has occurred, it's over. The bottom is in as far as I'm concerned on a probability basis. If we take out the lows, I'd be surprised, uh mainly because I continue to believe people are way too bearish relative to the reality of the earnings growth that's coming.

insights.claim: The four-day rally in the Nasdaq (QQQ) reached close to 10%, one of the largest such moves in the 17 years since the financial crisis and clustered with famous bottoms like Liberation Day, COVID and 2022, with the key distinction that this time price stayed above an upward-sloping 200-day moving average.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Above-200-day thrusts historically mark durable bottoms rather than bear-market rallies, arguing for buying dips instead of fading strength.

insights.claim: The S&P 500 broke out of a three-month May-to-July pennant with a four-day rate of change of 6% — the biggest in a year — and the rally itself was 6% larger than the entire prior three-month range, which Visser says makes it un-fadeable.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A breakout larger than the consolidation range it came from is a momentum-continuation signal; shorting the breakout is the low-expectancy side.
insights.quote: And guess what? The rally we had was 6% bigger than the entire range that we saw for that time period. That is not something to fade.

insights.claim: Breadth confirms a bull market rather than a narrow AI melt-up: every S&P sector is up on the year with the index +13%, and IWM, the NYSE Composite and the equal-weight S&P all made new all-time highs in the same week.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Broad-based new highs undercut the 'only seven stocks are holding it up' bear case and support staying long beyond mega-cap tech.

insights.claim: Korea is not the contagion source bears claim: the KOSPI 200 is up 61% year-to-date with the technology sector up 116% after its collapse, and on days when SK Hynix is slightly down the machinery and construction sectors are leading and holding gains.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Rotation within Korea rather than wholesale liquidation suggests the AI capex complex is broadening geographically instead of unwinding.

insights.claim: The panic never showed up in index or credit markets — the VIX is at its lowest since January, single-name vol has mean-reverted to pre-episode levels, and the CDX index behaved just like the VIX with no credit issues at all — so investors who bought S&P puts for contagion lost on both direction and volatility.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Confirms the drawdown was a leverage/factor event, not a solvency event, and that index-level hedges were the wrong instrument.

insights.claim: The collapse in 7-day realized volatility of tech-momentum and sector-neutralized momentum factors over six days signals that funds are now hedged or have cut gross, and vol-targeted funds and burned pod shops cannot re-lever quickly — setting up a low-volume summer rally that forces reluctant managers to chase.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Positioning-driven melt-up risk into a period when seasonality bears (September, midterms) keep managers underexposed.

themes.theme: Hedging AI With Factor Vol, Rate-of-Change and Breadth

insights.claim: Visser argues factor volatility has structurally decoupled from S&P index volatility because it embeds long-short gross leverage, so index puts no longer hedge an AI thematic book the way they used to.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Reprices the whole hedging stack: single-name, factor and dispersion hedges over cheap-looking index puts for AI-heavy portfolios.
insights.quote: using index puts is not going to work the way that it used to

insights.claim: Visser explicitly calls peak gross leverage, predicting long-short gross comes down over the next few years because AI compresses time, increases crowding, and lowers the Sharpe ratio of factor strategies.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A multi-year de-grossing regime means more frequent violent factor unwinds and structurally lower returns for crowded quant/pod strategies.
insights.quote: I'm making the call that we are at peak gross leverage and that we will see leverage come down over the course of the next few years

insights.claim: Visser expects factor volatility to remain structurally elevated, spending the rest of this year in a 25-30 band rather than returning to prior lows, using an equal weight of four factors (momentum, value, quality, beta).
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A permanently higher factor-vol floor changes position sizing, stop levels and the cost of running crowded quant books.
insights.quote: I think factor vol is structurally going to be higher. I don't think we're going back down here.

insights.claim: Visser's replacement risk model for AI exposure combines a 50-day rate of change on his 100-name global AI thematic index with internal breadth: a ~50% 50-day move guarantees a fall, risk starts growing above 20%, and the warning fires when high rate-of-change is joined by deteriorating breadth inside the 100 names.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A concrete, replicable trigger set for de-risking AI exposure that fired before the July momentum break.

insights.claim: Visser says the 252-day rate-of-change recession model that flagged September 2007 no longer works because exponential AI and software innovation have shortened cycles, so he replaced it with the AI-thematic rate-of-change plus breadth combination.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Traditional macro lead indicators may signal too late in an AI-compressed cycle; investors relying on them risk being systematically behind.

insights.claim: Acting on his own rate-of-change warning, Visser sold all of his Micron early and rotated into silver, Bitcoin and Eli Lilly, which held up or gained through July while the memory names fell violently.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Illustrates rotating out of parabolic AI beta into debasement and non-correlated assets to preserve dry powder for the flush.

insights.claim: Universal access to AI backtesting and portfolio optimization makes crowding worse, producing more bubbles, parabolas and speed crashes — a market-structure change Visser says is never going back to the way it was.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Expect a higher frequency of violent factor drawdowns; hedging cadence and rebalancing must speed up accordingly.

insights.claim: AI compresses market time as well as economic time — Visser notes July was the worst month for momentum in his entire dataset — meaning terminal values get harder to estimate and a company can re-rate from a 30 PE to a 20 PE very quickly, which he says is happening to Google right now.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Multiple compression risk is now a fast, discrete event rather than a slow grind; long-duration equity narratives can be repriced in weeks.
insights.quote: AI compresses economic time, but it it may also compress market time. The month of July for momentum was worse than any year over the data that I have.

themes.theme: AI Demand Data vs the Bear Narrative

insights.claim: Per Gavin Baker, the AI sell-off is disconnected from the quantitative data: he has found no real negative demand metric and not a single instance of deceleration — GPU availability, GPU rental pricing and DRAM spot prices are all accelerating.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser, citing Gavin Baker
insights.so_what: Gives a falsifiable checklist — GPU rental prices, availability, DRAM spot — to monitor before turning bearish on AI infrastructure.
insights.quote: Um not a single instance of deceleration, nothing. In fact, every metric rate is accelerating.

insights.claim: GPU rental economics are inflating, not deflating: a B200 cluster that rented around mid-$2 per GPU hour seven months ago is now expected to rent for just under $4 per GPU hour, undercutting the thesis that AI chips depreciate fast and have short useful lives.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser, citing Gavin Baker
insights.so_what: Rising rental rates support hyperscaler depreciation schedules and AI-infrastructure asset values — a direct rebuttal to the 'obsolescence' short case.
insights.quote: The same type of B200 cluster that rented around mid $2 per hour 7 months ago is now expected to rent for just under $4 per GPU hour.

insights.claim: Visser has bought a decent amount of Nvidia over the last three weeks, arguing it sits at the lowest forward PE of the past 10 years, has already taken its multiple compression, and benefits from Vera Rubin and token-per-watt requirements — a 'safer' AI name that will not double quickly but is one of the best risk-adjusted holdings.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: An explicit long with a valuation anchor: de-rated mega-cap AI hardware as the lower-beta way to stay exposed to accelerating compute demand.
insights.quote: Nvidia actually, as we record this, is at the lowest forward PE of the last 10 years. I've bought a decent amount of Nvidia over the course of the last 3 weeks.

insights.claim: Visser argues there will never be enough compute because adoption is still tiny — only a few hundred thousand people are running generative AI agents out of 8 billion — so demand is exponential against a physical supply that scales linearly.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser, citing Gavin Baker
insights.so_what: Frames compute as a structurally short commodity: buy the physical build-out rather than betting on a capex air pocket.
insights.quote: Guys, I say it all the time. There will never be enough compute, ever. We will continually be building compute.

insights.claim: Falling token-index readings are being misread as bearish; even the data provider says it is not bearish on the market, because more usage is simply shifting to open source, which does not imply Anthropic's revenues stop growing.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Token-share metrics are a flawed short trigger for closed-model AI revenue; do not size bearish AI trades off them.

insights.claim: Elon Musk on the SpaceX earnings call said the current limiting factor is memory, with memory output supply rising around 20% a year against demand rising 200% a year or higher — economics 101 implying sustained price increases.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser, quoting Elon Musk
insights.so_what: A 10x supply-demand gap is the cleanest pricing-power setup in the AI supply chain; memory pricing is the key variable to track.
insights.quote: The limiting factor currently is memory. The memory output is increasing by around 20% a year. So, supply is increasing by about 20% a year. The demand is increasing by 200% a year, maybe higher.

insights.claim: Visser's 'AI equals memory' thesis holds that more compute does not solve the bottleneck without more memory, and that memory becomes even more critical as consumer AI agents scale — making the moment memory supply catches up to compute the key signal to watch.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Gives an exit trigger for the memory trade — supply catching compute — rather than a price-based stop.

themes.theme: Earnings and Macro Confirmation of the AI Capex Cycle

insights.claim: This earnings season shows roughly 50% earnings growth with revenue growth at 15% across sectors, a trend that began in Q1 2025 when the AI trade went into full force despite tariff-driven sentiment worries.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Revenue acceleration, not just buybacks or margin tricks, underwrites the equity rally and makes contagion from a factor unwind unlikely.

insights.claim: Margins have expanded from 13% a year ago to 17% now, broadly and not just in technology, and Visser expects further expansion as AI adoption and AI agents spread.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Economy-wide AI margin lift is the mechanism that lets estimates keep rising even if top-line growth slows.

insights.claim: The PMI has soared from below 50 a year ago to nearly 60, with durable goods non-defense ex-aircraft also near that level, validating Visser's earlier out-of-consensus call that the AI trade would drive the PMI toward 60.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Macro-level confirmation that AI capex is a real industrial cycle, supporting industrials, power and chemicals exposure alongside chips.

insights.claim: Palantir's commercial revenue growth accelerated from 54% to 64% to 149% year-over-year — Q2 revenue of $764 million against $306 million a year earlier — with 220 deals of at least $1M, 98 of at least $5M and 78 of at least $10M, which Visser uses as the best public proxy for enterprise AI adoption given Anthropic and OpenAI do not report.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Accelerating growth off a rising base is the tell that AI agent adoption is inflecting; Palantir prints become a read-through for the whole enterprise AI complex.

themes.theme: Hyperscaler Capex Math and the Decay of Public Companies

insights.claim: Visser is not bullish on hyperscalers relative to the infrastructure trade because Goldman Sachs projections put group free cash flow turning positive far in the future, meaning Microsoft, Meta and Amazon keep spending on hope of revenue while facing heavy competition.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Prefer picks-and-shovels AI infrastructure over hyperscaler equity; the capex burn is a multi-year FCF drag.

insights.claim: Visser argues hyperscaler multiples deserve compression and their CDS deserve to be wider for justified reasons — they are leveraging up, cloud revenue alone will not cover it, and without new products they get priced like a utility or real estate company.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: The cleanest expression for shorting the AI trade is buying hyperscaler CDS rather than equity puts, especially while spreads keep widening.
insights.quote: whether their businesses will be there is a question, and that's why their multiples should be compressed, and their CDS should be wider

insights.claim: Jeff Dean leaving Google and Demis Hassabis moving to another area are, to Visser, a signal of internal conflict at a company that gives away products like AlphaFold for free while spending heavily and taking on debt, and needs actual consumer or corporate products to monetize.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Talent departures at big-tech AI labs are an early warning on monetization gaps and a reason Google's multiple is compressing now.

insights.claim: Visser is negative on all public companies by 2030 because bureaucracy will drive frustrated top talent out, while AI-native companies grow rapidly — new business formations are going parabolic and he dates the inflection to the release of Opus 4.5.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A structural short on incumbent public-equity profit pools and an argument for private/venture exposure to one-person AI companies.
insights.quote: It's reason why I'm negative on all public companies by the time we get to 2030, the bureaucracy is going to be a killer.

insights.claim: Visser's 'two printing presses' framework holds that government money printing debases the unit you measure wealth in while the AI printing press dilutes the durability of the corporate claims you bought to protect that wealth — the case for abundant intelligence and scarce Bitcoin.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Justifies owning scarce assets over both cash and long-duration equity claims; the core rationale linking his AI and crypto books.
insights.quote: Two printing presses running at once. One dilutes the unit you measure wealth in. That is the debasement of your money. The other dilutes the durability of the corporate claims you bought into to protect that wealth.

themes.theme: Yen Intervention, Warsh and the Fiscal Train

insights.claim: Visser reads the first coordinated US-Japan currency intervention since 1998 as a treasury-market defense: Scott Bessent is helping the BOJ so Japan does not have to sell its large Treasury holdings to buy yen, and is urging the Fed to help defend the yen and expand facility capacity.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: If the US is defending the yen to protect its own bond market, sovereign-debt stress is being managed with liquidity — bullish hard assets, bearish fiat.
insights.quote: Long view, US props up the yen to support treasuries.

insights.claim: Visser argues it will be very hard for Kevin Warsh to raise rates while the Fed is helping Japan, since defending the yen requires interest-rate differentials, and he is shocked the market still prices a 45% chance of a September hike (with 63% priced for the BOJ) after the payroll number.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A direct fade: rate-hike odds embedded in the curve are too high, which is the setup for the debasement trades to run.
insights.quote: we still have a 45% chance of a rate hike in September, which is why I like all the debasement trades, as I talked about a few weeks ago, thinking that people were getting way too over their skis on rate hikes

insights.claim: The intervention's financing adds liquidity when the punch bowl is already overflowing, and the Treasury has now spent all the ammunition in its exchange stabilization fund — meaning that without a change in interest-rate differentials the whole effort is wasted.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Exhausted FX ammunition plus added liquidity points to repeated interventions and more monetary accommodation, not less.
insights.quote: The way it is being financed is unprecedented and adds liquidity when the punch bowl of the US economy and markets is already overflowing.

insights.claim: Visser's 'nothing stops this train' framework says governments cannot let long yields run because falling equity values cut corporate tax receipts while deficits are already 5-6%, so 30-year yield spikes reliably precede official intervention and S&P rallies — July was the largest 30-year yield rise in a month during Trump's tenure and stocks rallied anyway.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Fading the 'bond yields will crash stocks' trade has been persistently profitable; the policy reaction function caps yields and supports equities.
insights.quote: So, the S&P has rallied when rates go higher because everyone starts getting bearish on it and the Fed or the Treasury needs to step in. Nothing stops this train.

insights.claim: Visser draws an explicit analogy between the current setup — situational awareness, Warsh's non-guidance, the coordinated BOJ move, and a historic month of deleveraging — and October 1998, arguing that as long as the lows hold this will be remembered as the moment markets realized the fiat system may be in trouble.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A 1998 analog implies a liquidity-driven melt-up in risk assets from here alongside a structural bid for hard assets.
insights.quote: when the US is intervening in the Japanese currency market to help their treasury market, the fiat system might be in trouble

themes.theme: Debasement Trades: Gold, Silver, Platinum, Bitcoin

insights.claim: Gold rose 7.2% for the week — the third biggest week in 16 years — and broke back above its 50-day moving average after the third-longest stretch below it, a bull-market consolidation-and-breakout pattern Visser says can run hard.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A technical trigger to re-enter gold after months of chop, driven by the market repricing Warsh as less hawkish.
insights.quote: This is a big week in gold, up 7.2%.

insights.claim: Visser sees an absolute reason to own gold, silver, platinum and Bitcoin together on the assumption that the Fed does not hike, with platinum breaking above its 50-day on a rounding chart and silver closing above its 50-day; he holds a good-sized silver position originally for AI demand and now also for debasement.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A basket expression of the debasement view with defined technical entries at the 50-day for each metal.

insights.claim: Speculative dollar positioning is at its highest long level even though the dollar has already broken down, which Visser calls fuel for the fire for gold, silver, platinum and Bitcoin.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Crowded dollar longs into a broken-down dollar create forced-unwind upside for hard assets.

insights.claim: Visser says Bitcoin remains technically in a bear market until it clears his resistance level and any exposure below it is a trading position, but he thinks the level holds and breaks out — noting Bitcoin was okay this week despite the Clarity Act's odds of being signed into law this year collapsing from near 50% to 17%, Michael Saylor's Strategy selling more, and a Coldcard cold-storage exploit.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Bitcoin absorbing three simultaneous negative catalysts without breaking is a resilience tell; the breakout level defines the risk.
insights.quote: Bitcoin is still in a bear market until we get above there.

themes.theme: Hidden Labor Weakness and Broken Inflation Data

insights.claim: Visser argues economists are missing labor-market weakness because low jobless claims are an artifact of a shrinking labor force: participation has fallen sharply this year, yet wages are not rising — the quits rate and Atlanta Fed wage growth are back at 2019 levels and average hourly earnings are down to 3.2%.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: If wages are decelerating with shrinking labor supply, the hawkish case is hollow and rates should fall — supporting the fade of September hike odds.
insights.quote: So, the supply of labor is going down because the labor force participation rate is coming down sharply, has come down sharply this year. Well, if there's less labor supply, shouldn't that mean wages are going higher?

insights.claim: Aggregate weekly payrolls — combining hours, average hourly earnings and job creation — just posted their weakest six-month rate of change going back to 2012 excluding COVID, and the only jobs created over the last 18 months have been in healthcare.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: The single hardest data point behind his dovish rates call; a metric to track monthly for the Fed-repricing trade.
insights.quote: When you strip out healthcare, there is no job creation. That is not a good jobs market.

insights.claim: Visser says AI is already suppressing hiring but not yet firing, and expects no large job-loss event because demographics and retirements absorb it — instead, one-employee million-dollar AI-native companies will gradually replace firms with 50-100 employees, keeping labor conditions structurally weak.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Implies a slow-bleed labor market that keeps rates capped without triggering a recession-style earnings collapse.
insights.quote: AI agents are have or AI is having an impact on hiring. It's not yet had an impact on firing

insights.claim: Truflation's core measure has made a violent move lower over the last four weeks and continues to fall year-over-year even as core CPI ticks up, leading Visser to call the inflation data a disaster and urge Warsh to look at Truflation and trimmed mean rather than a 50-year-old calculation methodology.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: If real-time inflation is collapsing while official CPI lags, the hawkish repricing is a fade and duration plus hard assets both win.
insights.quote: This is a violent move lower over the course of the last 4 weeks. So, the year-over-year Truflation number just continues to fall.

insights.claim: With 10-year yields currently above their 20-month moving average of 4.29 while labor force participation falls, Visser argues rates should be coming down, and expects weakness to eventually show up in either inflation or the AI-driven job market in a way that surprises people.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Sets 4.29 on the 10-year as the technical line for a duration long tied to his labor-weakness thesis.

insights.claim: Visser points to his college-age, non-computer-science son already running an AI chief of staff that spins out new sub-agents at his internship as evidence that agentic AI adoption is accelerating from the bottom up and is now a hiring differentiator.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Ground-level confirmation of the agent adoption curve that underwrites both the compute-shortage and labor-displacement theses.
insights.quote: I have my AI chief of staff spitting out new sub agents on the regular. This is what he's doing at his internship.
